title: What Are Tannins in Wine?
description: Tannins are natural wine compounds that create grip and drying texture. Learn where they come from, how they feel and how they differ from acidity, sweetness and bitterness.
text: Highlights Tannins are naturally occurring compounds found mainly in grape skins, seeds and stems. Oak can contribute tannin too. Tannin feels more like texture than taste: drying, gripping, firm, rough or puckering. Tannin is not the same as sweetness, acidity, alcohol, bitterness or body. Red wines generally have more noticeable tannin because their juice spends more time with grape skins and other solids. White and rosÃ© wines can contain tannin, especially when made with skin contact, seed contact or oak. Tannin can add structure and contribute to ageing potential, but more tannin does not automatically mean better wine. Australian Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir can all show tannin, but the style varies from wine to wine. Quick answer: what are tannins? Tannins are a group of naturally occurring phenolic compounds. In grapes, they are found mainly in the skins and seeds, with stems also contributing when they are included during winemaking. Oak can add another source of tannin as wine matures in barrels or with other oak products. When you drink a tannic wine, you may notice that your gums and the inside of your cheeks feel dry, grippy or slightly rough. This sensation is called astringency . It is often compared with the feeling left by strong black tea or the skin of an unripe fruit. Tannin is not simply a flavour. It is mainly experienced as a mouthfeel or texture. A wine can also taste bitter, but bitterness and astringency are different sensations. Red wines usually contain more noticeable tannin because their juice commonly ferments with grape skins, seeds and sometimes stems. White and rosÃ© wines generally have less extracted grape tannin, but they are not automatically tannin-free. Where does tannin come from? Grape skins Grape skins contain tannins and other phenolic compounds. During red-wine production, juice remains in contact with the skins during fermentation and macerationâ€”the period when juice and grape solids interact. This contact can extract tannin as well as colour and other compounds. Colour and tannin often develop together, but a deeply coloured wine is not necessarily more tannic. Grape seeds Grape seeds are another important source of tannin. Seed tannin can contribute bitterness or a more angular, drying sensation, although its effect depends on the grape, its ripeness, the winemaking and the rest of the wine. Seed tannin is not automatically harsh or undesirable. Stems and stalks Stems can contribute tannin when they are included during fermentation, as in some whole-bunch styles. The result depends on factors such as stem ripeness, the proportion used and how the wine is made. Oak Oak barrels and other oak products can contribute tannins, along with flavours and aromas such as vanilla, toast, spice or cedar. Oak-derived tannin is not exactly the same as grape-derived tannin, but both can influence a wineâ€™s structure and texture. Why do red wines usually have more tannin? In many red wines, fermentation takes place with grape skins and other solids still present. This gives the juice more opportunity to extract phenolic compounds, including tannins. The result is influenced by much more than contact time. Grape ripeness, fermentation conditions, temperature, pressing, alcohol development, seed and skin condition, stem inclusion and other winemaking decisions all matter. White wine is commonly pressed and separated from skins and seeds earlier, so it generally has less noticeable grape tannin. RosÃ© usually has shorter skin contact than red wine, but its tannin level can vary. A rosÃ© made with extended skin contact may feel more phenolic or grippy than a pale, briefly macerated style. What does tannin feel like? Try focusing on your gums and the inside of your cheeks after swallowing or spitting. Tannin may feel: drying; gripping; firm; rough; chalky or powdery; puckering; less smooth or lubricated. The sensation may build for a few seconds after the sip. Tannin can feel silky and fine in one wine, or coarse and aggressive in another. These are descriptions of texture, not automatic judgements about quality. Tannin versus bitterness Astringency is the drying or gripping mouthfeel associated with tannin. Bitterness is a taste sensation. Tannin can contribute to bitterness in some circumstances, but tannin is not the same thing as bitterness. Tannin versus dryness A tannic wine can feel drying, but a dry wine generally means a wine with little or no perceptible sweetness. These are separate ideas. A wine can be dry and tannic, dry and low in tannin, sweet and tannic, or sweet and low in tannin. Tannin versus acidity Acidity usually feels fresh, tart or mouth-watering. Tannin feels more like grip and drying texture. A wine can have both noticeable acidity and noticeable tannin; one is not the opposite of the other. Tannin versus alcohol and body Alcohol may feel warm or hot. Body describes the wineâ€™s overall weight and fullness in the mouth. Tannin can contribute to structure and substance, but it is not body itself. A light- or medium-bodied wine can still have noticeable tannin, while a full-bodied wine can have soft tannin. What do tannins feel like in Australian wines? Variety is a useful clue, not a guarantee. Australian Shiraz â€”the common Australian label term for Syrahâ€”can range from supple and medium-bodied to concentrated and firmly structured. Cabernet Sauvignon often provides a clear example of a wine with noticeable tannin and structure, but Australian Cabernet varies with region, vintage, ripeness and winemaking. Pinot Noir is often less tannic in impression than Cabernet Sauvignon, but it can still have clearly perceptible tannin. Skin contact, stem inclusion, ripeness, extraction and oak all influence the result. A grape variety or regional name cannot tell you everything about the tannin in an individual bottle. The wineâ€™s vintage, growing conditions, winemaking and maturation also matter. Do tannins soften with age? Maturation can change the way tannin feels. Some wines become less aggressively astringent or seem more integrated with time, as tannins and other components undergo chemical changes. However, tannins do not simply vanish, and ageing does not guarantee that every tannic wine will become softer or better. Tannin is one factor that can contribute to structure and ageing potential, alongside acidity, alcohol, fruit concentration, balance and storage conditions. More tannin is not automatically a sign of higher quality. A simple way to taste tannin You can try this with a small sip of red wine: Notice whether the wine is sweet or dry. Pay attention to its acidity: does it feel fresh or mouth-watering? Let the wine move naturally around your mouth. Focus on your gums and inner cheeks. Ask whether the wine feels smooth or drying, soft or gripping, silky or rough. Separate that sensation from alcohol warmth and bitterness. Compare the feeling with strong black tea if a reference helps. You do not need to assign the wine a precise tannin level. The aim is simply to recognise the sensation. Choosing a softer or more structured wine Words such as soft , supple and silky often suggest a less aggressive tannin sensation. Words such as firm , structured , grippy and chewy suggest more noticeable tannin. These descriptions are useful guides, not exact measurements. If you prefer less drying texture, ask a retailer or cellar-door host for a softer or more supple style. If you enjoy firmness and grip, ask for something more structured. For a refresher on tasting wine, see How to taste wine . You can also explore examples through Shiraz , Pinot Noir and Cabernet Sauvignon . Tannin FAQs Are tannins only found in red wine? No. Red wines usually show more noticeable tannin, but white and rosÃ© wines can contain tannin from grape solids, skin contact, seed contact, oak or other winemaking choices. Are tannins bitter? Tannin can contribute bitterness, but its main beginner-facing sensation is usually astringency: drying, gripping or puckering mouthfeel. How can I tell if a wine has tannin? Notice whether the wine makes your gums and cheeks feel dry, rough or grippy after the sip. Strong black tea offers a useful sensory comparison. Which Australian wines have the most tannin? There is no reliable universal ranking. Australian Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon can show noticeable tannin, while Pinot Noir can also be tannic depending on the wineâ€™s region, ripeness and winemaking. Does more tannin mean better wine? No. Tannin is a style and structural characteristic, not a score for quality. A wine can be enjoyable with firm tannin, soft tannin or very little noticeable tannin.

title: What Are Wine Grape Clones?
description: Wine grape clones are selected vine lines within a grape variety. Learn how clones differ from varieties and rootstocks, why growers use them and what they canâ€”and cannotâ€”tell you about wine style.
text: Highlights A grapevine clone is a selected vine reproduced through cuttings, buds or grafting. Clones belong to grape varieties such as Pinot Noir, Chardonnay or Shiraz. A clone is not the same as a rootstock: the clone provides the fruiting variety, while the rootstock provides the roots. Different clones may vary in ripening time, yield, bunch shape, berry size, vigour and health status. Clone choice can influence wine style, but it never determines the finished wine by itself. A clone number is not a guaranteed tasting note, quality score or prestige marker. Quick Answer: What Is a Wine Grape Clone? A wine grape clone is a group of grapevines descended through vegetative propagation from one selected parent vine. Instead of growing from seed, a vine is reproduced from a bud, cutting or grafted piece of the original plant. This preserves the selected vineâ€™s genetic identity with a high degree of similarity. The selected vine may have useful characteristics, such as a particular ripening time, yield, bunch structure, berry size or level of vigour. Once that material has been evaluated and multiplied, it may be identified as a clone within a grape variety. For example, Pinot Noir is a grape variety. A particular Pinot Noir clone is one selected line within that variety. Clone choice can affect how grapes grow and ripen, and may contribute to differences in the resulting wine. But the finished wine also reflects the vineyard site, climate, soil, rootstock, vine age, farming, vintage, harvest decisions and winemaking. The simplest way to think about it is: Variety + clone + site + season + farming + winemaking = finished wine A clone is one part of that equation, not the whole answer. Clone, Variety and Rootstock: Whatâ€™s the Difference? These terms describe different parts of a grapevine. Term Meaning Grape variety The broad named type of grape, such as Pinot Noir, Chardonnay or Shiraz Clone A selected line within a variety, reproduced from one parent vine Rootstock The root-forming part of a grafted vine Scion The upper, fruit-bearing part grafted onto the rootstock A vineyard might therefore use a particular Chardonnay clone grafted onto a particular rootstock. The clone supplies the fruiting variety. The rootstock forms the root system and can influence factors such as vigour, water access, soil adaptation and response to pests or conditions. A clone is also not a new grape variety. Pinot Noir remains Pinot Noir whether a vineyard uses one selection or another. Why Do Growers Use Different Clones? Grapevines have been cultivated and propagated for centuries. Individual vines within a variety can show natural differences. If one vine appears to have useful characteristics, growers or researchers can preserve those characteristics by reproducing it vegetatively. Clonal selection involves identifying, evaluating and multiplying selected vine material. Selection may consider: how early or late the grapes ripen; yield and crop consistency; bunch compactness; berry size; vine vigour; colour or phenolic development; disease sensitivity or resilience; suitability to a particular site or climate. These differences can matter in a vineyard planted for decades. An early-ripening selection may help in a cool region or short growing season. A later-ripening selection may suit a longer season or a site where growers want to avoid rapid sugar accumulation. Neither is automatically better. The right choice depends on the vineyardâ€™s conditions and the wine style the grower is trying to produce. How Can Clones Affect Grape Growing? Ripening Clones within the same variety may reach maturity at different times. That can affect harvest planning and the balance between sugar, acidity, flavour and phenolic maturity. The same clone will not necessarily ripen identically everywhere. Temperature, water availability, soil, crop level and seasonal weather all have an effect. Yield and bunch structure Clones may differ in productivity, bunch size, berry size and bunch compactness. A loose bunch and a compact bunch can create different airflow and disease conditions. Berry size can also change the relative amount of skin to juice. That may influence the raw material available for winemaking, but farming decisions and vintage conditions matter too. Vigour and site suitability A vineâ€™s apparent vigour is an interaction between clone, rootstock, soil, water, climate, planting density and vineyard management. A clone that performs well on one site is not automatically the best choice for another. This is one reason clone information is most useful when it is accompanied by context about the vineyard. Plant health Planting material also has an identity and health dimension. Growers want confidence that the material is the variety and selection it is claimed to be, and that it has been assessed for relevant health risks. Identity, health status and field performance are separate things. A vine can be correctly identified without being suited to every site, and certified planting material does not guarantee a particular wine style. How Can Clones Affect Wine Style? Clones can influence the grapes arriving at the winery. Differences in ripening time, berry and bunch structure, crop level or grape composition may contribute to differences in: acidity and sugar at harvest; colour potential; aroma-related compounds; tannin and phenolic development; texture; concentration. But these effects are conditional. The same clone can produce different wines in different regions, vintages or wineries. Conversely, wines from different clones may taste similar when they come from similar sites and are made in similar ways. This is why it is risky to translate a clone number directly into a tasting note. A named Pinot Noir clone does not guarantee floral aromas, and a named Chardonnay clone does not guarantee a particular texture or level of richness. Clone choice may help explain a growerâ€™s decisions. It cannot, by itself, explain the entire character of a wine. What Is Massal or Field Selection? Massal selection , also called field selection, involves taking propagation material from several desirable vines in an existing vineyard or population rather than multiplying one formally identified clone. This approach can preserve a broader range of genetic diversity and may help maintain heritage or locally adapted material. Formal clonal selection, by contrast, generally involves evaluating and documenting one selected line, including its agronomic and health characteristics. Neither approach is automatically superior. Clonal material may offer greater consistency and traceability. Massal selection may preserve diversity and history, but its identity and health status can be less uniform unless the material has been carefully tested and documented. What Does This Mean in Australia? Australia uses planting material from different propagation and selection systems. Clone names and numbers should not be treated as a universal international code: their meaning can depend on the variety, collection, nursery or identification system involved. Wine Australia is developing VitiCert Australia, a national certification programme for grapevine planting material. The programme is intended to improve confidence in vine identity and health across the propagation supply chain. It launched in 2026, with the first certified cuttings expected from winter 2028. That does not mean all Australian vine material is currently VitiCert-certified. The Australian Wine Research Institute also provides DNA-based grapevine clonal identification using a verified reference database. This reflects a practical issue: names and records are important, but identity can sometimes require scientific verification. Australia also maintains and develops collections of grape varieties, clones, rootstocks and heritage material. This work supports access to planting material with better-known identity and health status while helping preserve valuable older vines. How Should Wine Drinkers Interpret Clone Information? If a producer mentions a clone, you can reasonably understand it as information about a selected planting line within a grape variety. It may help explain: why the grower chose that material; how the vines suit a particular site; when the grapes tend to ripen; how the vineyard manages crop levels; why several selections may be blended. You should not assume that a clone name or number tells you: exactly how the wine will taste; whether the wine is better; whether the material is prestigious; whether it is certified or disease-free; whether it is used throughout a region; whether it expresses terroir more strongly. A useful question is: What does this clone information add to my understanding of the vineyard? If the producer explains the cloneâ€™s role in ripening, crop level or site suitability, it may be genuinely useful. If the label simply lists a number, there may not be enough information to turn it into a reliable flavour prediction. Frequently Asked Questions Are clones genetically identical? They are highly similar vegetative descendants of one selected vine, but â€œidentical in every wayâ€ is too absolute. Health status, propagation history, rootstock, vine age and growing conditions can all affect field performance. Is a clone the same as a variety? No. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are varieties. A clone is a selected line within one of those varieties. Is a clone the same as a rootstock? No. The clone normally refers to the fruiting part of the vine. The rootstock provides the root system beneath it. Does a clone determine a wineâ€™s flavour? No. A clone may contribute to grape composition and wine style, but site, climate, farming, vintage, harvest timing and winemaking also matter. Does certified planting material guarantee better wine? No. Certification can improve confidence in identity and health. It does not guarantee quality, flavour or commercial success. Why might a winery mention a clone? It may be giving context about vineyard material, ripening behaviour, site suitability or the way a wine was assembled. The meaning is strongest when the producer explains the clone alongside the vineyard and winemaking choices. The Takeaway A wine grape clone is a selected vine line reproduced from one parent vine. It sits within a grape variety and is separate from the rootstock. Clones can help growers manage ripening, yield, bunch structure, vine vigour and plant health. Those choices may influence the grapes and contribute to wine style. But a clone is not a flavour shortcut. To understand the wine in your glass, consider the whole picture: the variety, the clone, the site, the season, the farming and the winemaking.

title: What Does Oak Do to Wine?
description: Learn how oak can influence wine flavour, aroma, texture and ageing, and why not every oaked wine tastes the same.
text: Highlights Oak can change wine through wood-derived flavour and through the way wine matures in an oak vessel. Possible oak characters include vanilla, spice, toast, smoke, cedar and coconut. Oak can also affect texture, tannin and perceived body. New, small barrels usually make a more obvious impression than older, larger or neutral vessels. â€œOakedâ€ does not automatically mean sweeter, better or more expensive. Barrel fermentation and barrel maturation are related, but they are not the same thing. Australian Chardonnay, Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon can all be made with oakâ€”or without it. Quick Answer: How does oak affect wine? Oak affects wine in two main ways. First, wine extracts compounds from the wood. These can contribute aromas and flavours such as vanilla, spice, toast, smoke, char, cedar, coconut or caramel. Oak also contributes tannins that can affect bitterness, astringency and mouthfeel. Second, an oak barrel provides a particular environment for maturation. Because wood is porous, the wine can have limited, gradual interaction with oxygen. This can change colour, aroma, tannin structure and texture over time. Small amounts of oxygen may support some maturation reactions, especially in red wine, but too much oxygen can damage freshness and fruit character. So oak is not simply a flavouring. It is both a material that can contribute flavour and a vessel that can influence how wine develops. The result depends on the type of oak, whether it is new or used, the toast level, barrel size, time in contact with the wine and the wine itself. Fruit ripeness, acidity, alcohol, grape tannin, lees contact and bottle age also shape how oak is perceived. Oak flavour is only part of the story When people say a wine is â€œoakyâ€, they may be describing obvious aromas of vanilla, toast or smoke. Those impressions can come from compounds released by the wood, particularly after the inside of a barrel has been heated or toasted during manufacture. But oak influence is broader than aroma. Time in oak can also make a wine feel more textured, firm or rounded. In a red wine, oak-derived tannins may add structure or a drying sensation. In a white wine, barrel use may contribute weight or texture, particularly when combined with lees contact or stirring. These effects are not guaranteed. Oak does not automatically add body, soften every wine or improve its quality. A wineâ€™s alcohol, acidity, concentration and grape tannins may be just as important to the way it feels in your mouth. What do new, used and neutral oak mean? New oak New oak has not previously been used for wine. It contains more extractable compounds, so it generally contributes a stronger and more recognisable oak character. A wine matured in a small new barrel may show prominent vanilla, toast, spice or smoke. That can be an intentional style, but if the oak overwhelms the fruit, the wine may feel unbalanced. Used or seasoned oak Used, or seasoned, oak has already held wine and released some of its extractable compounds. It normally contributes less obvious flavour than new oak. That does not mean it does nothing. An older barrel can still influence the wineâ€™s oxygen environment, maturation, evaporation, lees contact and texture. It must also be carefully maintained, because poorly managed barrels can contribute unwanted taints. Neutral oak â€œNeutral oakâ€ is a practical wine-industry term for a vessel that contributes little obvious oak flavour. It is not necessarily chemically or structurally inactive. A winemaker may use neutral oak when they want some of the benefits of barrel maturation without making vanilla or toast the main feature. Why barrel size matters Barrel size changes the amount of wood surface area in contact with each litre of wine. A smaller barrel generally gives a greater relative wood contact and a faster, more noticeable oak influence than a larger vessel made from comparable wood. This is why a small new barrel may produce a more obvious oak style, while a large-format oak vessel or foudre can allow slower, subtler maturation. Larger vessels are not automatically â€œbetterâ€, and smaller barrels are not automatically more powerful in every circumstance. Barrel age, wood, toast, fill level, cellar conditions and the wine itself all matter. What does toasting do? Toasting means heating the inside of a barrel or oak product during manufacture. Heat changes the compounds available for extraction. Different toast levels can encourage different balances of fresh wood, vanilla, spice, toast, char and smoke. A heavily toasted barrel may offer more smoky or charred impressions, while other toast choices may emphasise sweeter spice or vanilla-like characters. However, toast level alone does not predict the final wine. Contact time, barrel size, oak species, previous use and wine composition also affect the result. â€œMore toastâ€ is not a simple synonym for â€œmore oakâ€. Barrel fermentation versus barrel maturation These terms describe different stages of winemaking. Barrel-fermented: fermentation takes place in an oak barrel. Barrel-aged or barrel-matured: wine spends time in an oak barrel after, or partly after, fermentation. Barrel-fermented and matured: both stages take place in oak. Barrel fermentation can affect the wine differently from fermenting in stainless steel and then transferring the wine to oak. It may also occur alongside lees contact, lees stirring or malolactic fermentation. This matters particularly for Chardonnay. A creamy, nutty or broad texture may reflect a combination of oak, lees and fermentation choicesâ€”not oak alone. Oak alternatives: chips, staves and inserts Winemakers can use oak products such as chips, cubes, staves or inserts to add wood-derived compounds to wine. These formats can provide oak aromas and phenolic effects, but they do not reproduce every feature of barrel maturation. A barrel combines wood contact with a vessel environment, gradual oxygen interaction, evaporation and the possibility of lees or sediment management. Oak alternatives primarily change the amount and type of wineâ€“wood contact. Some may be used alongside controlled oxygen techniques, but they are not identical to traditional barrel ageing. Australian wine regulations recognise oak and oxygen among inputs or techniques permitted under good manufacturing practice. That does not mean a label must disclose every technical detail of the format used. Terms such as â€œoakedâ€, â€œbarrel-agedâ€ and â€œunoakedâ€ should therefore be understood as useful style clues, not complete production records. How oak appears in Australian wine Australian producers use oak in many different ways rather than following one national oak style. Chardonnay may be barrel-fermented, matured in new or seasoned oak, made in larger-format barrels or produced without obvious oak influence. Some producers use oak and lees to build texture; others aim to preserve freshness and fruit. Shiraz may be matured in oak for structure and integration, with older barrels or larger vessels used when a producer wants subtler influence. Cabernet Sauvignon may also be matured in French or American oak, sometimes to help its firm tannins and oak character become more integrated. These are broad examples, not rules. No grape variety must be oaked, and Australian wine style is not defined by Australian-grown barrel wood. Australian wineries may use French, American, European or other oak sources, depending on the wine and the winemakerâ€™s choices. â€œAustralian oakâ€ is therefore not a synonym for â€œoak used in Australian wineâ€. For broader context, see How wine is made , and explore Chardonnay or Shiraz for variety-specific examples. How to taste oak without guessing You do not need to identify an exact aroma such as vanillin or guaiacol to notice oak. Try this: Smell the wine before swirling it, then swirl and smell again. Look for the overall impression: fresh fruit, spice, toast, smoke, cedar, creaminess or a drying finish. Taste the wine and notice whether the oak feels integrated with the fruit or sits on top of it. Pay attention to texture. Does the wine feel firmer, broader, more savoury or more drying? Compare it with an unoaked example if you can. A wine with prominent oak may show obvious toast, vanilla, smoke or drying wood-related tannin. A wine with restrained oak may show more subtle spice, texture or savoury complexity, with fruit still leading. A wine with no obvious oak influence may taste fresher and more direct, although it can still have plenty of body, structure and complexity. The same aroma descriptor can come from different sources, so tasting is about forming an impression rather than solving a laboratory test. Common questions about oak Does oak make wine taste sweet? Not necessarily. Vanilla, caramel and sweet spice aromas can create a sweet impression, but oak does not automatically add sugar. A dry wine can smell sweet without tasting sweet. Does oak make wine better? No. Oak is a stylistic and structural choice. Well-integrated oak can support a wine, while excessive oak can hide fruit and freshness. Unoaked wine can be deliberate, expressive and complex. Does oak soften tannins? Oak maturation can change tannin structure and the way tannin feels, but it does not soften every wine in the same way. The outcome depends on the wine, oxygen exposure, time and other winemaking choices. Is barrel-fermented wine heavily oaked? No. Barrel fermentation may be carried out in older or larger-format barrels, or balanced through blending. The term tells you where fermentation occurred, not how strong the oak flavour will be. Is unoaked wine less serious? No. â€œUnoakedâ€ usually signals an intention to preserve fruit, acidity and freshness. It says something about the winemaking approach, not the quality of the wine. title: What Does Yeast Do in Wine?
description: Yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat during fermentation. Learn how yeast affects wine aroma, texture and style.
text: Highlights Yeast drives alcoholic fermentation. It consumes grape sugars and produces alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat. Yeast also creates compounds that can influence a wineâ€™s aroma, flavour and texture. Saccharomyces cerevisiae is commonly the main yeast carrying fermentation through to completion. Cultured yeast and ambient fermentation are different winemaking approachesâ€”not automatically better or worse. Yeast fermentation is different from malolactic fermentation, which is performed by bacteria. The finished wine reflects yeast, grapes, vintage and winemaking conditions working together. Quick Answer Yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol during alcoholic fermentation. It also produces carbon dioxide, heat and many other compounds that can influence the finished wineâ€™s aroma, flavour and texture. A simple way to think about it is: Grape sugar + yeast activity â†’ alcohol + carbon dioxide + heat + other flavour-active compounds The process is more than a chemical conversion. As yeast works, it changes the grape juice into wine. The type of yeast, the fermentation conditions and what happens afterwards can all affect the result. Yeast does not create a wineâ€™s entire character by itself. Grape variety, vineyard, vintage, temperature, nutrients, oxygen, vessel and maturation also matter. Yeast is the engine of alcoholic fermentation, but the finished wine reflects the interaction between the yeast, the grapes and the winemaking choices. How Yeast Makes Alcohol Grape juice naturally contains fermentable sugars, principally glucose and fructose. Yeast consumes these sugars and converts much of them into ethanolâ€”the alcohol in wineâ€”and carbon dioxide. Fermentation also releases heat and produces other substances, including acids, glycerol, higher alcohols and aroma compounds. That is why fermentation can change grape juice in such a dramatic way: it alters not only the alcohol level, but also the smell, texture and overall shape of the wine. The carbon dioxide usually escapes during a still-wine fermentation. In sparkling wine, winemakers retain some of it so it becomes the bubbles. This is alcoholic fermentation. It is different from malolactic fermentation , a separate process in which bacteria convert sharper-tasting malic acid into softer-tasting lactic acid. Yeast drives alcoholic fermentation; bacteria drive malolactic fermentation. Why Saccharomyces cerevisiae Matters Many microorganisms may be present in grape juice and fermenting wine. However, Saccharomyces cerevisiae is commonly the main yeast that carries alcoholic fermentation through to completion. It is useful in winemaking because it can cope with several difficult conditions: high sugar, increasing alcohol, acidity, sulphur dioxide and limited oxygen. As fermentation progresses, these conditions become increasingly stressful. Yeasts that are less tolerant may decline, while S. cerevisiae often becomes dominant. That does not mean every fermentation is made up of one yeast species. Other yeasts can contribute earlier in the process or work alongside S. cerevisiae , particularly in ambient or mixed fermentations. Cultured Yeast and Ambient Fermentation Winemakers may add a selected cultured yeast , also called a commercial starter yeast, to grape juice. This gives the fermentation a deliberate starting point and can offer greater predictability, reliability and repeatability. Alternatively, a winemaker may allow fermentation to begin with microorganisms already associated with the grapes, winery or equipment. This is often called ambient , indigenous , uninoculated or wild fermentation. The terms overlap, but they do not mean that only one special â€œwild yeastâ€ is involved. Ambient fermentation can involve a changing community of yeasts and bacteria. Its variability may contribute different aromas or textures, but it can also make the fermentation less predictable. Cultured fermentation offers more control, but that does not mean it produces characterless wine. So, is one approach better? Not automatically. Australian producers use both cultured and ambient approaches, depending on the wine style, fruit, winery practice and the desired balance between reliability and microbial variation. â€œWildâ€ does not automatically mean more natural, complex or superior, just as commercial yeast does not automatically mean inferior or artificial. How Yeast Can Affect Aroma and Style Yeast produces compounds that contribute to fermentation-derived aroma. These can include fruity esters, higher alcohols, organic acids, aldehydes and sulphur compounds. Yeast can also transform compounds that came from the grapes into forms we can smell. Different yeast species and strains may therefore contribute different aromatic profiles. One fermentation might emphasise fresh fruit or floral notes, while another may show more savoury or fermentation-derived characters. The result depends on more than the yeastâ€™s name. Temperature, nutrients, oxygen, fermentation speed, grape chemistry and the presence of other microorganisms all influence what happens. Yeast can help shape a wineâ€™s style, but it does not determine the style on its own. A wineâ€™s aroma also comes from the grapes, oak, extraction, maturation and other cellar processes. It would be misleading to say that yeast creates every aroma in wine. Why Fermentation Conditions Matter Yeast does not work at exactly the same speed from beginning to end. Its environment changes as sugar is consumed and alcohol rises. Temperature Temperature affects yeast activity, fermentation speed and the balance of compounds produced. Different temperature conditions can therefore contribute to different sensory outcomes. If conditions become unsuitable, fermentation may slow or stop. Nutrients Yeast needs nutrients to grow and keep fermenting. An inadequate supply can contribute to sluggish or incomplete fermentation and can affect the compounds produced during fermentation. Oxygen Yeast may need some oxygen during its growth phase, while alcoholic fermentation later proceeds largely under oxygen-limited conditions. Oxygen exposure can affect yeast health and fermentation performance, as well as the wineâ€™s broader chemistry. Alcohol and sugar stress As alcohol accumulates, it becomes harder for yeast to remain active. High sugar, acidity, sulphur dioxide, limited nutrients and low yeast vitality can add further stress. A slow or stopped fermentation is not necessarily caused by â€œbad yeastâ€; it can result from several pressures acting together. What Happens to Yeast After Fermentation? After fermentation, inactive yeast cells can settle to the bottom of a tank or barrel as lees . Some wines remain in contact with their lees after fermentation. Over time, the breakdown of yeast cellsâ€”called autolysisâ€”can contribute to texture and savoury, bready or biscuity characters. This is particularly relevant in some sparkling and white-wine practices, but lees contact is a separate post-fermentation choice. It is not the same as yeast actively converting sugar into alcohol. What This Means When You Taste Wine When a wine smells fruity, floral, spicy, savoury or slightly bready, yeast may be part of the storyâ€”but it is only part. You do not need to identify a yeast strain to enjoy the wine. It is more useful to understand that fermentation choices can help explain why two wines made from similar grapes may smell or feel different. Yeast, fermentation conditions and maturation can give the winemaker several ways to influence the finished style. Frequently Asked Questions Does all wine contain yeast? Yeast is involved in the production of most wines because alcoholic fermentation is normally yeast-driven. Finished wine may contain little or no active yeast, particularly after clarification, filtration or settling. Is wild fermentation better than using commercial yeast? No approach is automatically better. Ambient fermentation can bring microbial variation and potential complexity, while cultured yeast can provide greater reliability and control. The result depends on the fruit, winery and intended style. Does yeast make wine sweet? Yeast consumes fermentable sugar. If fermentation finishes with little sugar remaining, the wine may taste dry. If some sugar remains, the wine may taste sweeter. Sweetness can also be managed through winemaking decisions, so yeast alone does not explain every sweet wine. Is yeast the same as the bacteria in malolactic fermentation? No. Yeast drives alcoholic fermentation, converting sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Malolactic fermentation is a separate bacterial process that changes malic acid into lactic acid. Can yeast make wine taste different? Yes. Yeast can produce and transform aroma-active compounds, and different strains or microbial communities can contribute different aromas and textures. Grapes and the wider winemaking process remain important influences too. Continue Learning How wine is made Winemaking What is sparkling wine?

title: What Is Acidity in Wine?
description: Learn what acidity in wine tastes like, how it differs from pH, sweetness and tannin, and how variety, climate and winemaking shape freshness and balance.
text: Highlights Acidity gives wine freshness, liveliness and a mouth-watering sensation. You may notice it as tartness, similar to the effect of citrus or green apple. Acidity is not the same as sweetness, tannin, sourness or pH. A high-acid wine is not automatically better, and a low-acid wine is not automatically faulty. Grape variety, ripeness, climate, harvest timing, winemaking and ageing can all influence acidity. You can recognise acidity by noticing how much your mouth waters and how fresh the wine feels. Quick Answer Acidity in wine is the presence and effect of naturally occurring acids that make wine feel fresh, lively and mouth-watering. It is one of wineâ€™s main structural components, working alongside sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit flavour and body. When acidity is noticeable, a wine may taste crisp, bright or energetic. It can create a tart sensation, rather like biting into a green apple or tasting citrus. A wine with less noticeable acidity may feel softer, rounder or broader. Neither style is automatically better. Acidity needs to make sense in the wine as a whole. It can keep a sweet wine from seeming heavy, give a rich white wine freshness, or help a red wine feel energetic rather than broad. But too much, too little or poorly integrated acidity can make a wine seem sharp, flat or unbalanced. How Does Acidity Feel? Acidity is easiest to recognise on the palate rather than by looking at the wine. Take a sip and notice whether your mouth begins to water. Does the wine feel refreshing and lively, or soft and broad? Does that freshness continue into the finish? Wine writers may describe acidity as: High-acid: acidity is clearly prominent. Low-acid: acidity is less noticeable. Crisp: fresh and lively, often with noticeable acidity. Soft: rounder or less obviously acidic. Flabby: an informal term for wine that seems to lack freshness or structural energy. These are descriptions, not quality scores. A crisp Riesling and a soft, full-bodied red can both be enjoyable when their acidity suits the style. Acidity can also feel like tension or energy. It gives the wine shape and movement rather than allowing it to seem static. However, the sensation is affected by temperature, sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit flavour and the person tasting it. Mouth-watering is a useful clue, not a laboratory test. Acidity Is Not the Same as Sourness or Sharpness Acidity can contribute to sourness or tartness, but the words do not mean exactly the same thing. Acidity is the chemical property and the related sensory quality. Sourness is a taste perception that may be caused by acids. Tartness is a common way of describing the fresh, sour-edged sensation acidity can create. Sharpness is an informal description. It may mean that the acidity feels especially prominent or aggressive, but it is not a precise technical term. A wine can have noticeable acidity without tasting unpleasantly sour. The final impression depends on how much acidity is present, the types of acids involved and how the acidity interacts with the wineâ€™s other components. Acidity, pH and Titratable Acidity Wine professionals use measurements to describe acidity, but those measurements are not identical to what you experience while drinking. pH is a chemical measurement related to the strength or activity of acidity in a solution. A lower pH indicates a more acidic chemical environment, but it does not perfectly predict how sour or refreshing a wine will taste. Titratable acidity , often shortened to TA, estimates the amount of acid that can react during a laboratory titration. It is commonly expressed as grams per litre of tartaric-acid equivalent. Perceived acidity is the experience of tasting the wine: how fresh, tart, lively or mouth-watering it feels. These measurements are related, but they are not interchangeable. Sweetness, alcohol, tannin, flavour concentration and texture can all change how acidity is perceived. This is why a number on a laboratory report cannot tell you exactly how a wine will feel in your mouth. How Acidity Interacts with Other Parts of Wine Acidity does not work alone. Sweetness Sweetness can make acidity seem less prominent, while acidity can stop a sweet wine from feeling heavy or cloying. Sweetness does not remove acidity; it changes how the two are experienced together. A dry wine with noticeable acidity may seem particularly crisp. A sweet wine with both richness and refreshing acidity can feel balanced rather than syrupy. Alcohol and Body Alcohol and body can make a wine feel broader, warmer or rounder, which may make its acidity seem less obvious. A lighter-bodied wine with similar acidity may feel brisker. This is not a fixed rule. The overall impression depends on the wineâ€™s fruit, texture and structure. Tannin Tannin is a separate sensation. It can feel drying, grippy or slightly rough, especially in red wine. Acidity feels more tart, fresh and mouth-watering. The two can appear together. A red wine with firm acidity and tannin may feel structured and energetic, while a wine with noticeable tannin but less acidity may feel drying without feeling particularly fresh. Fruit Flavour Fruit character changes how acidity is interpreted. Citrus, green apple and some red-fruit flavours may reinforce a fresh impression. Riper tropical or dark-fruit flavours can make a wine seem fuller, even when it still has substantial acidity. Ripe fruit does not automatically mean low acidity. What Influences Acidity? Several factors shape the acidity of a finished wine. Grape variety and ripeness Different grape varieties have different natural acid profiles and differ in how well they retain acidity as they ripen. As grapes ripen, sugar generally increases while some acids decline, although the pattern varies with variety and growing conditions. Harvest timing is therefore a decision about the relationship between sugar, acidity, flavour and texture. An early harvest is not automatically better, and a late harvest is not automatically low-acid. Climate and vineyard conditions Cooler conditions can help grapes retain acidity, while warmer conditions may accelerate ripening and acid loss. But climate does not determine a wineâ€™s acidity by itself. Variety, site, vintage, water availability, vineyard management, harvest decisions and winemaking also matter. This is one reason Australian wine cannot be described as having one acidity profile. The countryâ€™s regions, elevations, varieties and climates produce a wide range of styles. Fermentation and malolactic fermentation Some wines undergo malolactic fermentation, in which sharper-tasting malic acid is converted into softer-tasting lactic acid. This can make a wine feel rounder, but it does not simply remove all acidity. The choice to use or avoid this process is one of many winemaking decisions that can affect texture and the way acidity is perceived. For more on the wider winemaking process, see How wine is made . Ageing Acidity can help a wine retain freshness as it develops, but acidity alone does not guarantee that a wine will improve or last for a long time. Ageing also depends on the wineâ€™s other components, its style, storage and bottle condition. How Acidity Appears in Different Wines Acidity can be present in white, red, rosÃ© and sparkling wine. White wine: acidity may be especially easy to notice because white wine usually has little tannin and is often served chilled. It can make the wine feel crisp or citrusy. Red wine: acidity helps shape the relationship between fruit, alcohol and tannin. It may be less obvious in a full-bodied or strongly tannic wine. RosÃ©: acidity can support a fresh, dry style and help fruit flavours feel light rather than heavy. Sparkling wine: acidity works with carbon dioxide and sweetness to create freshness and lift. These are broad observations, not rules for every bottle. Australian Examples Australian Riesling is often a clear example of acidity supporting vibrant fruit and freshness. Adelaide Hills wines are also often described in terms such as lively and crisp. Southern Highlands Sauvignon Blanc can show good acidity. These descriptions are tendencies, not guarantees. Australian wine includes everything from bright, high-acid styles to softer, fuller wines with less prominent acidity. Warm-region wines can also retain balancing acidity, depending on variety, site, vintage, harvest timing and winemaking. The important lesson is not to judge acidity from a region name alone. Even two wines made from the same variety in the same region can feel different. A Simple Acidity Tasting Exercise Try this the next time you open a bottle: Take a small sip. Let the wine move naturally across your palate. Notice whether your mouth waters. Ask whether the wine feels fresh and lively or soft and broad. Notice whether the sensation continues into the finish. If possible, compare it with another wine. Describe the acidity separately from whether you like the wine. You do not need to identify a number. â€œFresh and mouth-wateringâ€ is already a useful observation. Frequently Asked Questions Is high acidity good in wine? Not automatically. High acidity can make a wine refreshing and energetic, but balance depends on how it works with sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit and body. Is acidity the same as sweetness? No. Acidity creates freshness and tartness, while sweetness creates a sense of sugar or richness. They can balance each other but are separate sensations. Is acidity the same as tannin? No. Acidity is usually felt as freshness, tartness and mouth-watering. Tannin is more often felt as dryness, grip or astringency. Are Australian wines high in acidity? There is no single Australian acidity style. Different varieties, regions, climates, vintages and winemaking choices produce different profiles. Does acidity mean a wine will age well? Acidity can help a wine retain freshness during ageing, but it does not guarantee longevity or improvement. Other components and storage conditions matter too. How can I tell if a wine has acidity? Take a sip and notice whether it makes your mouth water and feels fresh or lively. Compare it with a softer wine if you can.

title: What Is Balance in Wine?
